final_method_items.summary: Register the specialization SPEC as a specialization of TMPL with the indicated ARGS. IS_FRIEND indicates whether the specialization is actually just a friend declaration. ATTRLIST is the list of attributes that the specialization is declared with or NULL when it isn't. Returns SPEC, or an equivalent prior declaration, if available. We also store instantiations of field packs in the hash table, even though they are not themselves templates, to make lookup easier.
final_method_items.reason: Best fit to the reproducer. The crash pattern centers on distinct `std::array` and related library template specializations being created in one partition, then reused through later imports. This function is the core specialization bookkeeping path, and a bad registration/merge across BMIs would naturally cause deferred ICEs when later partitions or `<chrono>`-driven iterator machinery look the specialization up again.

final_method_items.signature: static tree retrieve_specialization (tree tmpl, tree args, hashval_t hash)
final_method_items.summary: Retrieve the specialization (in the sense of [temp.spec] - a specialization is either an instantiation or an explicit specialization) of TMPL for the given template ARGS. If there is no such specialization, return NULL_TREE. The ARGS are a vector of arguments, or a vector of vectors of arguments, in the case of templates with more than one level of parameters. If TMPL is a type template and CLASS_SPECIALIZATIONS_P is true, then we search for a partial specialization matching ARGS. This parameter is ignored if TMPL is not a class template. We can also look up a FIELD_DECL, if it is a lambda capture pack; the result is a NONTYPE_ARGUMENT_PACK.
final_method_items.reason: Very strong candidate because the failure appears deferred across `hewwo -> uwu -> owo`, which is exactly the pattern of imported specialization state being looked up later and found in an inconsistent form. If BMI-imported specializations are missing, mismatched, or only partially reconstructed, this lookup can return the wrong node or no node and trigger later crashes.

final_method_items.summary: Preload common nodes into CACHE and make sure they are merged properly according to the gimple type table.
final_method_items.reason: This is the strongest candidate because the failure pattern points to imported tree state surviving one module edge but becoming inconsistent after a second partition import. `preload_common_nodes` is directly responsible for pre-seeding and merging shared nodes during streaming-in, so a mistake here could easily yield wrong canonical/common nodes that only blow up later during template lookup or `<chrono>`-driven instantiation.

The bug report suggests imported declarations/specializations from different partitions are merged inconsistently, and that kind of corruption could survive one boundary and crash only when a later partition forces more work.

behavior_items: The reproducer exercises C++20 modules with a three-unit partition/import chain, conceptually `hewwo -> uwu -> owo`, where each later unit depends on declarations and imported state produced by the earlier unit. The report strongly suggests that the crash only appears once template-related information must flow through more than one module boundary, not just a single import edge.

The first module unit (`hewwo`) includes `<chrono>` and also causes at least one standard library template specialization to be formed, such as a concrete `std::array<...>` object. Including `<chrono>` is important because that header pulls in a large web of library declarations, iterators, traits, inline functions, and dependent templates, making the module interface/state much richer than a minimal header set.

A second unit (`uwu`) imports `hewwo` and introduces another specialization or alias involving a different `std::array` type. The key detail is that this is not merely reusing the exact specialization already instantiated in `hewwo`; it asks the compiler to reason about a related but distinct template instantiation while relying on imported declarations from the prior module unit.

A third unit (`owo`) then imports `uwu` and either declares another different `std::array` object, re-exports the imported partition, or in the third variant includes `<chrono>` again and triggers iterator-related library machinery instead of adding another array object. This means the failing path is not limited to one exact declaration form; several front-end actions over the imported module graph can trigger it.

The observed behavior is an internal compiler error (SIGSEGV), so the reproducer is not demonstrating bad user code or a rejected program. It is demonstrating that GCC reaches an invalid internal state while processing legal module imports and template instantiations across partitions.

The crash is highly sensitive to where `<chrono>` is included. When only the first unit has `<chrono>` and later units do not, GCC crashes. When all three units include `<chrono>`, the crash disappears. That strongly indicates a bug in how GCC serializes, imports, or lazily re-materializes template- or declaration-related state from module files, rather than a semantic problem with the source program itself.

The fact that adding `<chrono>` to `uwu` can move the crash point from `export import :uwu;` to `export import :owo;` indicates the failure is deferred. GCC is able to get past one module import boundary once enough local context is present, but later fails when another partition must consume or re-export the same imported template metadata.

Similarly, removing the distinct array instantiation from `uwu` changes where the crash happens rather than eliminating the general issue. That suggests the extra specialization in the middle partition is acting as a trigger for early instantiation/import work, but the underlying corruption or missing state persists until some later unit forces GCC to inspect it.

The report notes that `export` versus non-`export` on the declarations does not materially change the result. This is important because it narrows the issue away from symbol visibility rules and toward common machinery shared by both exported and non-exported declarations, such as template specialization bookkeeping, entity merging, and module attachment of declarations.

Crash 1 shows GCC failing when `hewwo` and `owo` both involve concrete `std::array` variables of different element counts/types, while `uwu` contributes an alias to yet another array specialization. This stresses multiple distinct specializations of the same primary template being known in different partitions and merged through imports.

Crash 2 shows that even an `export import :uwu;` path can be enough to trigger the ICE. That means GCC can fail without needing a complicated expression or use-site in the importing partition; simply re-exporting a partition that carries problematic imported template state is sufficient.

Crash 3 is especially revealing because `owo` reportedly contains no new array declaration at all, only `<chrono>` and some iterator-related machinery, yet GCC still crashes. This implies the root issue is broader than `std::array` object emission alone; the important part is likely that the imported module state contains template/dependent library entities that later standard-library processing expects to be complete and well-attached.

Because `<chrono>` drags in iterator and range-adjacent support indirectly, crash 3 suggests GCC is mishandling imported declarations needed by later template instantiation in the standard library. An imported specialization or associated declaration may be incomplete, duplicated, attached to the wrong module, or missing some companion node when later library templates attempt lookup or substitution.

The bug appears tied to cross-partition template instantiation ownership: one partition creates or imports a specialization, a later partition creates a different specialization of the same template family, and another partition subsequently consumes standard-library facilities that expect all related declarations to be consistently present. GCC instead reaches a null or invalid internal pointer and segfaults.

The reproducer therefore exercises several compiler subsystems at once: module interface serialization, partition import/re-export, declaration merging across BMIs, lazy template instantiation, and standard library template expansion from `<chrono>`. The ICE indicates a front-end defect in coordinating those subsystems, especially when imported template state is only partially reconstructed in downstream partitions.

The overall pattern from all three crashes supports the reporter's intuition that the exact visible symptom may vary, but the common trigger is the combination of: a template specialization formed in an early partition with `<chrono>` available, a different specialization or alias introduced in a middle partition without matching header context, and a later partition that forces GCC to revisit that imported state. When every partition includes `<chrono>`, each unit has enough local declarations to avoid the broken import path, masking the bug.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer stresses GCC's C++20 modules implementation by sending standard-library template state through a three-partition chain and then forcing additional template work in later partitions. `hewwo` imports `<chrono>` and forms template specializations, `uwu` introduces a different but related `std::array` specialization or alias without `<chrono>`, and `owo` either adds another specialization, re-exports the partition, or merely triggers more library template processing via `<chrono>`. GCC should import and merge that module/template information cleanly, but instead it segfaults, which points to a front-end bug in module BMI import/serialization and template instantiation bookkeeping rather than invalid user code. The strongest signal is that adding `<chrono>` to every partition avoids the crash, implying GCC mishandles imported standard-library declarations or specializations when downstream partitions rely on them without recreating the same header context locally.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: Common pattern: the crash is triggered only when template-related standard library state created in one module partition must be consumed again after passing through at least one more partition. The first unit builds rich template/declaration state by including `<chrono>` and forming concrete `std::array`-related entities; a later unit introduces a different specialization or alias of the same template family without recreating the same header context; a third unit then either re-exports that partition or performs more standard-library template work and GCC segfaults. Because adding `<chrono>` to all partitions makes the ICE disappear, and because `export` vs non-`export` does not matter, the shared failure mode is most consistent with broken module-state persistence rather than visibility rules or bad source. The likely compiler bug is that GCC's C++ front end leaves imported template/declaration metadata only partially reconstructed across partition boundaries, so later lookup/instantiation/merge code dereferences a missing or stale node. The three variants suggest the same underlying defect can surface during direct declaration processing, `export import` handling, or later iterator/traits instantiation from `<chrono>`, all of which depend on consistent specialization ownership and declaration attachment across BMIs.
possible_causes: Bug in C++20 modules BMI serialization/deserialization for template specializations or aliases: GCC may fail to write or lazily reload all companion data for imported `std::array`/library template specializations created in an earlier partition, leading to a null or dangling internal tree node when a downstream partition instantiates related templates.

Defect in declaration merging across module partitions: imported declarations or specializations from `hewwo` may be attached to the wrong module, duplicated, or merged incompletely in `uwu`/`owo`, so later front-end code sees an inconsistent specialization set for the same primary template and crashes during lookup or completion.

Bug in lazy template instantiation across partition chains: the middle partition's distinct specialization/alias appears to trigger deferred work, and the crash moving from `uwu` to `owo` suggests GCC is postponing instantiation/import until a later use point where required template arguments, declarations, or canonical types were never fully materialized.

Incorrect handling of standard-library entities introduced by `<chrono>` in module context: `<chrono>` pulls in iterators, traits, inline functions, and dependent templates, so GCC may mishandle imported dependent declarations associated with those headers when the importing partition does not include the same header textually, causing invalid lookup/substitution state.

Fault in `export import`/partition re-export processing for imported template metadata: crash 2 shows that merely re-exporting a partition can ICE, implying GCC may not correctly propagate or mark transitive imported specializations/declarations before another partition consumes them.

Canonical type or specialization identity mismatch across BMIs: multiple different `std::array` specializations formed in different partitions may not be recognized as belonging to one coherent template family after import, leading later code in template substitution, type comparison, or specialization lookup to follow invalid links and segfault.
evidence: The failure requires a three-unit chain `hewwo -> uwu -> owo`, which points to state surviving one import but breaking after transitive re-consumption across another partition boundary.
`hewwo` includes `<chrono>` and forms template-heavy library state; later partitions often omit `<chrono>`, and that omission is exactly when GCC crashes.

Including `<chrono>` in all three units consistently avoids the ICE, which strongly suggests missing or incompletely imported declarations are being papered over by rebuilding the same library context locally.

`export` versus non-`export` does not change the outcome, so the issue is unlikely to be pure export visibility logic and more likely shared machinery such as declaration attachment, specialization bookkeeping, or module import state.

Changing `uwu` by adding `<chrono>` or removing the extra distinct array specialization moves the crash point rather than removing the fundamental problem, which is typical of deferred/lazy import or instantiation bugs.
Crash 2 happens on `export import :uwu;` alone, showing GCC can fail while propagating imported module/template state even without a complex use-site in the importing partition.

Crash 3 does not require a new array declaration in `owo`; iterator-related machinery from `<chrono>` is enough to trigger the ICE, indicating the root defect is broader than object emission and likely involves imported dependent declarations used by later library templates.

All variants involve different specializations or aliases of the same standard template family spread across partitions, which is a classic stress pattern for specialization identity, canonical type merging, and transitive BMI reconstruction.

selected_files.reason: Most directly implicated: the crash depends on transitive C++20 module partition import/re-export (`hewwo -> uwu -> owo`), moves between import boundaries, and disappears when later partitions rebuild header context locally, which strongly points to broken module BMI import/export, entity remapping, or declaration attachment logic in the C++ modules front end.

The reproducer stresses template specialization identity and deferred instantiation across module boundaries using distinct `std::array` specializations and later `<chrono>`-driven library instantiations; this file owns core template instantiation and pending-template handling that could dereference incomplete imported specialization state.

Crash 3 suggests later library template processing in downstream partitions cannot consistently find or merge imported declarations from earlier BMIs; module-aware binding tables and merged global/module lookup state live here, making it a strong suspect for stale or incomplete imported declaration lookup.

The failure can occur while merely declaring another variable or alias in a later partition, indicating declaration completion/merging of imported template entities may be corrupt; this file handles variable declarations, type completion, and related front-end state that can trip on malformed imported nodes.

If the bug is incomplete reconstruction of imported template/declaration trees from BMIs, the read-side generic tree deserialization layer is a likely contributor, especially because the crash appears only when downstream partitions rely on imported state instead of reparsing the same headers.

The matching write-side tree streaming logic is also suspicious because a missing field or wrong canonicalization during module/BMI emission could survive one import and only crash when a later partition forces deeper template use.

Shared tree streaming cache and node identity machinery can cause exactly the kind of stale, duplicated, or mismatched tree nodes suggested by a SIGSEGV during transitive module import of related template specializations.

The report suggests imported declarations or types may be only partially reconstructed or attached to the wrong owning context; C++-specific tree construction and manipulation here could expose null or inconsistent nodes during later template/type processing.

As the low-level tree node infrastructure, this file is a secondary suspect if module import leaves invalid canonical type or declaration links that later front-end code follows while processing standard-library templates.

Lower probability than the C++ front-end files, but still plausible because GCC modules rely on streamer-style deserialization machinery; if imported module data is being read with missing companion state, the failure may surface here during reconstruction of trees used by later template instantiation.

When an importer needs to instantiate that template, they /must have/ the partial, explicit & extern specializations available. If they have the other specializations available, they'll have less work to do. gcc/cp/pt.cc.summary: Take the tree structure T and replace template parameters used therein with the argument vector ARGS. IN_DECL is an associated decl for diagnostics. If an error occurs, returns ERROR_MARK_NODE. Issue error and warning messages under control of COMPLAIN. Note that we must be relatively non-tolerant of extensions here, in order to preserve conformance; if we allow substitutions that should not be allowed, we may allow argument deductions that should not succeed, and therefore report ambiguous overload situations where there are none. In theory, we could allow the substitution, but indicate that it should have failed, and allow our caller to make sure that the right thing happens, but we don't try to do this yet. This function is used for dealing with types, decls and the like; for expressions, use tsubst_expr or tsubst_copy.

This function attempts to match PARM with ARG in a manner consistent with the existing assignments in TARGS. If more values are deduced, then TARGS is updated. Returns 0 if the type deduction succeeds, 1 otherwise. The parameter STRICT is a bitwise or of the following flags: UNIFY_ALLOW_NONE: Require an exact match between PARM and ARG. UNIFY_ALLOW_MORE_CV_QUAL: Allow the deduced ARG to be more cv-qualified (by qualification conversion) than ARG. UNIFY_ALLOW_LESS_CV_QUAL: Allow the deduced ARG to be less cv-qualified than ARG. UNIFY_ALLOW_DERIVED: Allow the deduced ARG to be a template base class of ARG, or a pointer to a template base class of the type pointed to by ARG. UNIFY_ALLOW_INTEGER: Allow any integral type to be deduced. See the TEMPLATE_PARM_INDEX case for more information. UNIFY_ALLOW_OUTE

LEN indicates the number of parameters we should consider (defaulted parameters should not be considered). The 1998 std underspecified function template partial ordering, and DR214 addresses the issue. We take pairs of arguments, one from each of the templates, and deduce them against each other. One of the templates will be more specialized if all the *other* template's arguments deduce against its arguments and at least one of its arguments *does* *not* deduce against the other template's corresponding argument. Deduction is done as for class templates. The arguments used in deduction have reference and top level cv qualifiers removed. Iff both arguments were originally reference types *and* deduction succeeds in both directions, an lvalue reference wins against an rvalue reference and otherwise the template with the more cv-qualified argument wins for that pairing (if neither is more cv-qualified, they both are equal). Unlike regular deduction, after all the arguments have been d

The TREE_PURPOSE is the innermost set of template parameters for the partial specialization. PAT2 is similar, but for the second template. Return 1 if the first partial specialization is more specialized; -1 if the second is more specialized; 0 if neither is more specialized. See [temp.class.order] for information about determining which of two templates is more specialized.

For example, suppose we have: template <class T, class U> struct S {}; template <class T> struct S<T*, int> {}; Then, suppose we want to get `S<double*, int>'. SPEC_TMPL will be the partial specialization and the ARGS will be {double*, int}. The resulting vector will be {double}, indicating that `T' is bound to `double'.

gcc/cp/pt.cc.summary: TEMPLATES is a TREE_LIST. Each TREE_VALUE is a TEMPLATE_DECL. Return the TREE_LIST node with the most specialized template, if any. If there is no most specialized template, the error_mark_node is returned. Note that this function does not look at, or modify, the TREE_PURPOSE or TREE_TYPE of any of the nodes. Since the node returned is one of the elements of INSTANTIATIONS, callers may store information in the TREE_PURPOSE or TREE_TYPE of the nodes, and retrieve it from the value returned.

If DECL is a specialization of some template, return the most general such template. Otherwise, returns NULL_TREE. For example, given: template <class T> struct S { template <class U> void f(U); }; if TMPL is `template <class U> void S<int>::f(U)' this will return the full template. This function will not trace past partial specializations, however. For example, given in addition: template <class T> struct S<T*> { template <class U> void f(U); }; if TMPL is `template <class U> void S<int*>::f(U)' this will return `template <class T> template <class U> S<T*>::f(U)'.

The result is cached in the TI_PARTIAL_INFO of the corresponding TEMPLATE_INFO unless RECHECKING is true. If the choice of partial specialization is ambiguous, a diagnostic is issued, and the error_mark_node is returned. If there are no partial specializations matching TARGET, then NULL_TREE is returned, indicating that the primary template should be used.

gcc/cp/decl.cc.signature: static void wrap_temporary_cleanups (tree init, tree guard)
gcc/cp/decl.cc.summary: We're initializing a local variable which has a cleanup GUARD. If there are any temporaries used in the initializer INIT of this variable, we need to wrap their cleanups with TRY_CATCH_EXPR (, GUARD) so that the variable will be cleaned up properly if one of them throws. Unfortunately, there's no way to express this properly in terms of nesting, as the regions for the temporaries overlap the region for the variable itself; if there are two temporaries, the variable needs to be the first thing destroyed if either of the temporary destructors throws. However, we only want to run the variable's cleanup if it actually got constructed. So we need to guard the temporary cleanups with the variable's cleanup if they are run on the normal path, but not if they are run on the exceptional path. We implement this by telling honor_protect_cleanup_actions to strip the variable cleanup from the exceptional path. Another approach could be to make the variable cleanup region enclose initialization, but depend on a flag to indicate that the variable is initialized; that's effectively what we do for arrays. But the current approach works fine for non-arrays, and has no code overhead in the usual case

On entry, DECL_INITIAL (decl1) should be NULL_TREE or error_mark_node, or may be a BLOCK if the function has been defined previously in this translation unit. gcc/cp/tree.cc.summary: Make a variant of TYPE, qualified with the TYPE_QUALS. Handles arrays correctly. In particular, if TYPE is an array of T's, and TYPE_QUALS is non-empty, returns an array of qualified T's. FLAGS determines how to deal with ill-formed qualifications. If tf_ignore_bad_quals is set, then bad qualifications are dropped (this is permitted if TYPE was introduced via a typedef or template type parameter). If bad qualifications are dropped and tf_warning is set, then a warning is issued for non-const qualifications. If tf_ignore_bad_quals is not set and tf_error is not set, we return error_mark_node. Otherwise, we issue an error, and ignore the qualifications. Qualification of a reference type is valid when the reference came via a typedef or template type argument. [dcl.ref] No such dispensation is provided for qualifying a function type. [dcl.fct] DR 295 queries this and the proposed resolution brings it into line with qualifying a reference. We implement the DR. We also behave in a similar manner for restricting non-pointer types.
Return TYPE with const and volatile removed.

gcc/cp/tree.cc.signature: tree strip_typedefs (tree t, bool *remove_attributes , unsigned int flags )
gcc/cp/tree.cc.summary: Builds a qualified variant of T that is either not a typedef variant (the default behavior) or not a typedef variant of a user-facing type (if FLAGS contains STF_USER_VISIBLE). If T is not a type, then this just dispatches to strip_typedefs_expr. E.g. consider the following declarations: typedef const int ConstInt; typedef ConstInt* PtrConstInt; If T is PtrConstInt, this function returns a type representing const int*. In other words, if T is a typedef, the function returns the underlying type. The cv-qualification and attributes of the type returned match the input type. They will always be compatible types. The returned type is built so that all of its subtypes recursively have their typedefs stripped as well. This is different from just returning TYPE_CANONICAL (T) Because of several reasons: If T is a type that needs structural equality its TYPE_CANONICAL (T) will be NULL. TYPE_CANONICAL (T) desn't carry type attributes and loses template parameter names. If REMOVE_ATTRIBUTES is non-null, also strip attributes that don't affect type identity, and set the referent to true if any were stripped.

gcc/cp/tree.cc.summary: Like strip_typedefs above, but works on expressions (and other non-types such as TREE_VEC), so that in template<class T> struct A { typedef T TT; B<sizeof(TT)> b; }; sizeof(TT) is replaced by sizeof(T).

gcc/cp/tree.cc.signature: tree copy_binfo (tree binfo, tree type, tree t, tree *igo_prev, int virt)
gcc/cp/tree.cc.summary: Makes a copy of BINFO and TYPE, which is to be inherited into a graph dominated by T. If BINFO is NULL, TYPE is a dependent base, and we do a shallow copy. If BINFO is non-NULL, we do a deep copy. VIRT indicates whether TYPE is inherited virtually or not. IGO_PREV points at the previous binfo of the inheritance graph order chain. The newly copied binfo's TREE_CHAIN forms this ordering. The CLASSTYPE_VBASECLASSES vector of T is constructed in the correct order. That is in the order the bases themselves should be constructed in. The BINFO_INHERITANCE of a virtual base class points to the binfo of the most derived type. ??? We could probably change this so that BINFO_INHERITANCE becomes synonymous with BINFO_PRIMARY, and hence remove a field. They currently can only differ for primary virtual virtual bases.

We force T's value to be within range of T's type (by setting to 0 or 1 all the bits outside the type's range). We set TREE_OVERFLOWED if, OVERFLOWED is nonzero, or OVERFLOWABLE is >0 and signed overflow occurs or OVERFLOWABLE is <0 and any overflow occurs We return a new tree node for the extended wide_int. Wrap a SAVE_EXPR around EXPR, if appropriate. Do this to any expression which may be used in more than one place, but must be evaluated only once. Normally, expand_expr would reevaluate the expression each time. Calling save_expr produces something that is evaluated and recorded the first time expand_expr is called on it. Subsequent calls to expand_expr just reuse the recorded value. The call to expand_expr that generates code that actually computes the value is the first call *at compile time*. Subsequent calls at compile time* generate code to use the saved value. This produces correct result provided that *at run time* control always flows through the insns made by the first expand_expr before reaching the other places where the save_expr was evaluated. You, the caller of save_expr, must make sure this is so. Constants, and certain read-only nodes, are returned with no SAVE_EXPR because that is safe. Expressions containing placeholders are not touched; see tree.def for an explanation of what these are used for.

Subroutine of stabilize_reference; this is called for subtrees of references. Any expression with side-effects must be put in a SAVE_EXPR to ensure that it is only evaluated once. We don't put SAVE_EXPR nodes around everything, because assigning very simple expressions to temporaries causes us to miss good opportunities for optimizations. Among other things, the opportunity to fold in the addition of a constant into an addressing mode often gets lost, e.g. "y[i+1] += x;". In general, we take the approach that we should not make an assignment unless we are forced into it - i.e., that any non-side effect operator should be allowed, and that cse should take care of coalescing multiple utterances of the same expression should that prove fruitful.

Stabilize a reference so that we can use it any number of times without causing its operands to be evaluated more than once. Returns the stabilized reference. Create a complex type whose components are COMPONENT_TYPE. If NAMED is true, the type is given a TYPE_NAME. We do not always do so because this creates a DECL node and thus make the DECL_UIDs dependent on the type canonicalization hashtable, which is GC-ed, so the DECL_UIDs would not be stable wrt garbage collection.
If TYPE is a real or complex floating-point type and the target does not directly support arithmetic on TYPE then return the wider type to be used for arithmetic on TYPE. Otherwise, return NULL_TREE.

Return OP, stripped of any conversions to wider types as much as is safe. Converting the value back to OP's type makes a value equivalent to OP. If FOR_TYPE is nonzero, we return a value which, if converted to type FOR_TYPE, would be equivalent to converting OP to type FOR_TYPE. OP must have integer, real or enumeral type. Pointers are not allowed! There are some cases where the obvious value we could return would regenerate to OP if converted to OP's type, but would not extend like OP to wider types. If FOR_TYPE indicates such extension is contemplated, we eschew such values. For example, if OP is (unsigned short)(signed char)-1, we avoid returning (signed char)-1 if FOR_TYPE is int, even though extending that to an unsigned short would regenerate OP, since the result of extending (signed char)-1 to (int) is different from (int) OP.

Return OP or a simpler expression for a narrower value which can be sign-extended or zero-extended to give back OP. Store in *UNSIGNEDP_PTR either 1 if the value should be zero-extended or 0 if the value should be sign-extended.

Returns true if T is, contains, or refers to a type with variable size. For METHOD_TYPEs and FUNCTION_TYPEs we exclude the arguments, but not the return type. If FN is nonzero, only return true if a modifier of the type or position of FN is a variable or parameter inside FN. This concept is more general than that of C99 'variably modified types': in C99, a struct type is never variably modified because a VLA may not appear as a structure member. However, in GNU C code like: struct S { int i[f()]; }; is valid, and other languages may define similar constructs.

Return value of a constant X and sign-extend it.

If TYPE is an integral or pointer type, return an integer type with the same precision which is unsigned iff UNSIGNEDP is true, or itself if TYPE is already an integer type of signedness UNSIGNEDP. If TYPE is a floating-point type, return an integer type with the same bitsize and with the signedness given by UNSIGNEDP; this is useful when doing bit-level operations on a floating-point value.

If TYPE is an integral or pointer type, return an integer type with the same precision which is unsigned, or itself if TYPE is already an unsigned integer type. If TYPE is a floating-point type, return an unsigned integer type with the same bitsize as TYPE.

reviewed_methods.summary: Register the specialization SPEC as a specialization of TMPL with the indicated ARGS. IS_FRIEND indicates whether the specialization is actually just a friend declaration. ATTRLIST is the list of attributes that the specialization is declared with or NULL when it isn't. Returns SPEC, or an equivalent prior declaration, if available. We also store instantiations of field packs in the hash table, even though they are not themselves templates, to make lookup easier.
reviewed_methods.reason: Best fit to the reproducer. The crash pattern centers on distinct `std::array` and related library template specializations being created in one partition, then reused through later imports. This function is the core specialization bookkeeping path, and a bad registration/merge across BMIs would naturally cause deferred ICEs when later partitions or `<chrono>`-driven iterator machinery look the specialization up again.

reviewed_methods.signature: static tree retrieve_specialization (tree tmpl, tree args, hashval_t hash)
reviewed_methods.summary: Retrieve the specialization (in the sense of [temp.spec] - a specialization is either an instantiation or an explicit specialization) of TMPL for the given template ARGS. If there is no such specialization, return NULL_TREE. The ARGS are a vector of arguments, or a vector of vectors of arguments, in the case of templates with more than one level of parameters. If TMPL is a type template and CLASS_SPECIALIZATIONS_P is true, then we search for a partial specialization matching ARGS. This parameter is ignored if TMPL is not a class template. We can also look up a FIELD_DECL, if it is a lambda capture pack; the result is a NONTYPE_ARGUMENT_PACK.
reviewed_methods.reason: Very strong candidate because the failure appears deferred across `hewwo -> uwu -> owo`, which is exactly the pattern of imported specialization state being looked up later and found in an inconsistent form. If BMI-imported specializations are missing, mismatched, or only partially reconstructed, this lookup can return the wrong node or no node and trigger later crashes.

reviewed_methods.summary: Preload common nodes into CACHE and make sure they are merged properly according to the gimple type table.
reviewed_methods.reason: This is the strongest candidate because the failure pattern points to imported tree state surviving one module edge but becoming inconsistent after a second partition import. `preload_common_nodes` is directly responsible for pre-seeding and merging shared nodes during streaming-in, so a mistake here could easily yield wrong canonical/common nodes that only blow up later during template lookup or `<chrono>`-driven instantiation.

reviewed_methods.signature: tree duplicate_decls (tree newdecl, tree olddecl, bool hiding, bool was_hidden)
reviewed_methods.summary: If NEWDECL is a redeclaration of OLDDECL, merge the declarations. If the redeclaration is invalid, a diagnostic is issued, and the error_mark_node is returned. Otherwise, OLDDECL is returned. If NEWDECL is not a redeclaration of OLDDECL, NULL_TREE is returned. HIDING is true if the new decl is being hidden. WAS_HIDDEN is true if the old decl was hidden. Hidden decls can be anticipated builtins, injected friends, or (coming soon) injected from a local-extern decl.
reviewed_methods.reason: Strong candidate because module imports and template instantiations often converge through redeclaration merging. The bug report suggests imported declarations/specializations from different partitions are merged inconsistently, and that kind of corruption could survive one boundary and crash only when a later partition forces more work.

reviewed_methods.signature: static void record_common_node (struct streamer_tree_cache_d *cache, tree node)
